description: The Earth produces enough food to feed every human being. So why do **800 million people** around the world still go hungry?

hero.hook: The hunger of 800 million people is not a problem of food, but of sharing.

blocks.text: About **800 million people** go hungry in the world today, one person in ten. The figure is all the stranger because humanity has never produced so much food: statistically, there is far more than enough to feed everyone.
So hunger is not a problem of quantity but of distribution. Understanding global food security means understanding how abundance and famine can live side by side on the same planet.

According to the **[[Food and Agriculture Organization]]** of the United Nations, chronic undernourishment still affected about 800 million people in 2024. That global figure hides very different realities. The worst-hit areas lie in sub-Saharan Africa, where more than a quarter of the population regularly lacks food, and in South Asia.

blocks.caption: Hunger still reaches hundreds of millions of people, above all in sub-Saharan Africa

blocks.text: Food distress takes several forms. **Undernourishment** means a lack of calories. **Micronutrient deficiencies**, often called “hidden hunger,” affect 2 billion people who lack essential vitamins or minerals, with consequences for growth and health. **Malnutrition**, surprisingly, also covers obesity: in many developing countries, people are slowly swapping fresh produce for processed food, rich in calories and poor in nutrients.
If the world cut its food waste by just 25%, the food saved would in theory be enough to feed every one of the 800 million people who go hungry today.

The world currently produces the equivalent of 2,800 kilocalories per person per day, far more than enough to end hunger. The real problem is not shortage but **access**: the poorest people simply cannot afford food whose price keeps swinging on world markets.

The other side of this paradox is **waste**. About a third of world production, some 1.3 billion tons of food, is lost every year. In poor countries the losses come early: too few places to store crops, no cold rooms, roads in bad shape. In rich countries the waste comes later, at the point of distribution and consumption.
Since the 2010s, obesity and diseases linked to excess weight have killed more people worldwide each year than undernutrition, a historic turning point for global public health.

sections.title: The paradox of abundance and waste

blocks.text: Food security is also a matter of geopolitics. Many countries depend on exports from a handful of farming powers, which leaves them very exposed to the slightest blockage. Ukraine and Russia together supply almost 30% of world wheat exports. When that flow stops, prices soar on the Chicago **[[futures market]]**, where coming harvests are traded, and countries such as Egypt or Lebanon slide into a severe social crisis.

This fragility also comes from a choice made in the 1960s: the **[[Green Revolution]]**. That wave of new farming techniques pushed yields sharply up, but it also narrowed the variety of crops and left farmers dependent on chemical fertilizer. As a result, every rise in the price of oil feeds straight into the price of bread.
The idea of **food power** describes exactly this: using food exports on purpose as diplomatic leverage, or even as a sanction against a rival country.

sections.title: When food becomes a geopolitical weapon

blocks.text: By 2050 the world population should reach 10 billion. Climate change already threatens yields by multiplying droughts and floods, and by shifting where crops can grow. Intensive farming also wears out soils and underground water tables, which sometimes empty faster than they refill.

One promising path is **[[agroecology]]**: producing food by working with natural cycles, such as compost and crop rotation, instead of fighting them with chemicals. The goal is to guarantee every human being permanent access to healthy food, without draining the planet further.
The Earth produces enough calories to feed everyone. The hunger of 800 million people therefore comes from problems of access, waste and geopolitical crises, made worse by climate change.

sections.title: Feeding 10 billion people without exhausting the planet
